To endeavour means to try seriously and sincerely to do something, especially something that is difficult, important, or requires sustained effort. That is the heart of it.

But that one sentence doesn't capture the full picture, so let's go deeper.

Not all tries are equal. When you say you will endeavour to do something, you are not making a casual, throwaway attempt. You are signalling genuine commitment, purposeful effort, and earnest intent. The word carries a sense of dignity and seriousness.

Think of it this way:

  • "I'll try to call you later." → Casual, relaxed, no strong commitment implied.
  • "I will endeavour to resolve this matter promptly." → Serious, sincere, implies real effort and dedication.

The word endeavour sits closer to a promise of effort than a simple attempt. It tells the listener: I mean this. I am putting real energy into this.
What It Does and Does Not Guarantee

This is important: endeavouring to do something does not mean you will succeed.

The word describes the effort, not the outcome. You can endeavour to climb a mountain and still not reach the top. You can endeavour to win a competition and still lose. The focus is entirely on how seriously and sincerely you are trying, not on whether you get there.

This makes it an honest word. It commits to effort without overpromising a result.

The verb endeavour almost always follows this pattern:

endeavour + to + [verb]

You endeavour to do something. Always followed by an infinitive (the "to + verb" form).

Examples of correct usage:

  • "I will endeavour to finish the report by Friday."
  • "She endeavoured to keep her composure during the argument."
  • "The team is endeavouring to find a lasting solution."
  • "He endeavoured to understand her point of view."
  • "We endeavour to deliver the highest quality service."

You would not say: "I endeavoured completing it." The "to + verb" structure is essential.

Tenses work normally:

  • Present: I endeavour to help.
  • Past: She endeavoured to help.
  • Future: We will endeavour to help.
  • Continuous: They are endeavouring to help.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding a word clearly often means knowing how it differs from its neighbours.

Try — The everyday, neutral, all-purpose word. You can "try" anything — a new food, a joke, a difficult task. It carries no particular weight or formality. Try is the plain, default word for making an attempt.

Attempt — More formal than try, and it tends to describe a single, specific act. You "attempt" one thing in one moment — an exam, a jump, a difficult task. It doesn't strongly imply ongoing or sustained effort.

Strive — This word is intense. It suggests fighting hard against difficulty, struggling, pushing through obstacles. It is more emotionally charged and dramatic than endeavour.

Endeavour — Sits in a distinct space of its own. It is more sincere and weighty than try, more sustained and dignified than *attempt, and less dramatically intense than *strive. It is the word of calm, serious, committed effort. It is what a professional, an institution, or a person of integrity uses when they mean business — but without theatrics.
The Register: When and Where This Word Lives

Endeavour is a formal word. You will not typically hear it in casual everyday conversation between friends. It belongs to:

  • Professional and business writing: "We will endeavour to process your request within 48 hours."
  • Official correspondence and documents: "The committee endeavoured to represent all stakeholders fairly."
  • Literature and formal speeches: "She endeavoured, with every ounce of her will, to remain silent."
  • Customer service language: "Our staff will always endeavour to assist you."

If you used it in a casual conversation, it would sound stiff or overly formal — like wearing a tuxedo to a picnic. It is not wrong, but it is unusual.

One more thing: Endeavour is the British English spelling. In American English, the same word is spelled endeavor (without the 'u'). The meaning and usage are completely identical — only the spelling differs.
A Set of Rich, Varied Examples

Reading a word in many different contexts is one of the best ways to truly own it.

  1. "The doctors endeavoured to save his life throughout the night." (serious, sustained, high-stakes effort)
  2. "Despite the chaos, she endeavoured to maintain order in the classroom." (effort in the face of difficulty)
  3. "I will always endeavour to be honest with you, even when it is hard." (a sincere personal commitment)
  4. "The young writer endeavoured to capture the feeling of loss in her first novel." (earnest creative effort)
  5. "The organization endeavours to support vulnerable communities across the country." (ongoing, principled institutional effort)
  6. "He had endeavoured to apologise, but she had already left." (effort that did not succeed — note that the outcome failed, but the effort was real)

To endeavour (verb) is to make a sincere, serious, and purposeful effort to achieve something — especially something difficult — with no guarantee of success, and with a tone that is formal, dignified, and committed.

That is the complete picture of the word. You now know not just what it means, but how it feels, how it works grammatically, where it lives, and exactly how it differs from every word that might look like its twin.
